subproblems.title: An embedded submanifold is Borel and meets small closed balls in compact sets
subproblems.statement: Let P, r, d ∈ ℕ and M ⊆ ℝ^P with IsEmbeddedSubmanifold r d M, i.e. every y ∈ M has open sets V ⊆ ℝ^d and W ⊆ ℝ^P with y ∈ W and a map ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^P that is C^r on V and injective on V, with ψ(V) = W ∩ M, V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) compact for every compact K ⊆ W, and Dψ(v) injective for v ∈ V. Then (a) M is a (Borel) measurable subset of ℝ^P, and (b) every y ∈ M has some ε > 0 such that M ∩ closedBall(y, ε) is compact.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P r d : ℕ) (M : Set (Euclid P)), IsEmbeddedSubmanifold r d M → MeasurableSet M ∧ ∀ y ∈ M, ∃ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε ∧ IsCompact (M ∩ closedBall y ε)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 2 of the supplied parent proof ("M ∩ closedBall y (2ρ₁) = ψ(V ∩ ψ⁻¹(closedBall y (2ρ₁))) is compact"), together with the measurability of M that the parent needs for the integrals ∫_M. Only continuity of ψ on V, ψ(V) = W ∩ M and the properness of the charts are used.
1. (Compact slices of a chart.) Let y ∈ M and let (V, W, ψ) be a chart at y given by IsEmbeddedSubmanifold r d M. Claim: for every compact K ⊆ W the set M ∩ K is compact. First, M ∩ K = ψ(V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K)). Indeed, if x ∈ M ∩ K then x ∈ W because K ⊆ W, so x ∈ W ∩ M = ψ(V); write x = ψ(v) with v ∈ V, and then v ∈ V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K). Conversely, for v ∈ V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) we have ψ(v) ∈ ψ(V) = W ∩ M ⊆ M and ψ(v) ∈ K. Next, V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact by the properness clause of the chart, and ψ is continuous on V (a C^r map on V is continuous there, for every r ≥ 0), hence continuous on V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K). The continuous image of a compact set is compact, so M ∩ K is compact.
2. (Part (b).) W is open and y ∈ W, so there is r' > 0 with ball(y, r') ⊆ W. Put ε := r'/2 > 0. Then closedBall(y, ε) ⊆ ball(y, r') ⊆ W, and closedBall(y, ε) is compact because ℝ^P is a proper metric space. By step 1, M ∩ closedBall(y, ε) is compact.
3. (An open set containing M.) For each y ∈ M choose a chart (V_y, W_y, ψ_y) at y, and let O := ⋃_{y ∈ M} W_y. O is open, being a union of open sets, and M ⊆ O because y ∈ W_y.
4. (M = O ∩ closure(M).) The inclusion M ⊆ O ∩ closure(M) is clear from step 3. Conversely, let p ∈ O ∩ closure(M). Pick y ∈ M with p ∈ W_y and r' > 0 with ball(p, r') ⊆ W_y. The set C := M ∩ closedBall(p, r'/2) is compact by step 1 (closedBall(p, r'/2) is compact and contained in ball(p, r') ⊆ W_y), hence closed. Since ball(p, r'/2) is open, ball(p, r'/2) ∩ closure(M) ⊆ closure(ball(p, r'/2) ∩ M), and p belongs to the left-hand side. Hence p ∈ closure(ball(p, r'/2) ∩ M) ⊆ closure(C) = C ⊆ M.
5. (Part (a).) By step 4, M is the intersection of the open set O and the closed set closure(M). Open and closed sets are Borel, so M is measurable.

Source: step 1 of the parent proof (Simon Ch. 6, §1: coordinate covectors dx^I and the pairing of Λⁿ with Λₙ). The Cauchy–Binet identity is proved inline.
Notation:
- e_0, …, e_{P−1} is the standard basis of ℝ^P (EuclideanSpace.basisFun), and v(i) is the i-th coordinate of v ∈ ℝ^P.
- Λⁿ := Covector (Euclid P) n, the continuous alternating n-linear maps (ℝ^P)^n → ℝ; Λₙ := MultiVector P n = Λⁿ →L[ℝ] ℝ.
- 𝓘 is the finite set of strictly increasing I : Fin n → Fin P, and e_I := (e_{I(0)}, …, e_{I(n−1)}).
- For α ∈ Λⁿ, |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α = (Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} α(e_I)²)^{1/2}. The defining sum runs over all I : Fin n → Fin P, with term α(e_I)² for strictly increasing I and 0 otherwise, so it is the same sum.
- For v = (v_0, …, v_{n−1}) ∈ (ℝ^P)^n and I ∈ 𝓘, v^I is the n×n matrix with (k, j) entry v_j(I(k)).
1. (Coordinate covectors.) For I ∈ 𝓘 let dx^I ∈ Λⁿ be dx^I(v) := det(v^I). It is n-linear and alternating in v, because the determinant is multilinear and alternating in its columns and column j, (v_j(I(k)))_k, depends linearly on v_j. It is continuous because ℝ^P is finite-dimensional. In SimonGMT (Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter06.FormsDuality), dx^I = wedgeCovectors n (fun k ↦ EuclideanSpace.proj (I k)), and wedgeCovectors_apply_det gives exactly this formula. For n = 0, dx^I is the constant covector 1, the determinant of the empty matrix.
2. (Kronecker property.) For I, J ∈ 𝓘, dx^I(e_J) = 1 if I = J and dx^I(e_J) = 0 if I ≠ J. The matrix (e_J)^I has (k, j) entry 1 if I(k) = J(j) and 0 otherwise. If I = J it is the identity matrix. If I ≠ J, the ranges differ, because a strictly increasing map Fin n → Fin P is the increasing enumeration of its range. Both ranges have n elements, so some I(k) is not in range J. Row k of (e_J)^I is then zero, and the determinant is 0.
3. (Expansion.) For every α ∈ Λⁿ and v ∈ (ℝ^P)^n: α(v) = Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} α(e_I)·dx^I(v).
 Both sides are alternating n-linear functions of v; the right side is a linear combination of the dx^I. By multilinearity, two n-linear maps on ℝ^P agree once they agree on every basis tuple e_f := (e_{f(0)}, …, e_{f(n−1)}), f : Fin n → Fin P.
 - If f is not injective, both alternating maps vanish at e_f, which has a repeated entry.
 - If f is injective, let J ∈ 𝓘 enumerate range f increasingly, and let σ be the permutation of Fin n with f = J ∘ σ. By alternation, each side at e_f equals sign(σ) times its value at e_J. At e_J the right side is Σ_I α(e_I) dx^I(e_J) = α(e_J) by step 2.
 Hence the two sides agree.
4. (Sum of squared minors; Cauchy–Binet.) For every orthonormal family τ = (τ_0, …, τ_{n−1}) in ℝ^P, Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} det(τ^I)² = 1. This is the Cauchy–Binet formula det(AᵀA) = Σ_I det(A_I)² for the P×n matrix A with columns τ_j, where AᵀA = Id. Self-contained derivation:
 - Let δ_τ ∈ Λⁿ be δ_τ(v) := det(⟨τ_i, v_j⟩)_{i,j}. It is n-linear, alternating and continuous for the same reasons as dx^I, and equals wedgeCovectors n (fun i ↦ ⟨τ_i, ·⟩).
 - By orthonormality, δ_τ(τ) = det(⟨τ_i, τ_j⟩) = det(Id) = 1.
 - δ_τ(e_I) = det(τ_i(I(j)))_{i,j} = det((τ^I)ᵀ) = det(τ^I), and dx^I(τ) = det(τ^I).
 - Step 3 with α = δ_τ and v = τ gives 1 = δ_τ(τ) = Σ_I δ_τ(e_I)·dx^I(τ) = Σ_I det(τ^I)².
5. (Proof of (a).) Let ξ, Q satisfy IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q, with orthonormal τ and sign s, so ξ(α) = s·α(τ) for all α. For α ∈ Λⁿ, step 3 and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in ℝ^𝓘 give
 |ξ(α)| = |α(τ)| = |Σ_I α(e_I) det(τ^I)| ≤ (Σ_I α(e_I)²)^{1/2}·(Σ_I det(τ^I)²)^{1/2} = |α|·1,
 using step 4.
6. (Definition of L.) For ζ ∈ Λₙ put L(ζ) := Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} ζ(dx^I)·dx^I. Each ζ ↦ ζ(dx^I) is evaluation at a fixed point, a continuous linear functional on Λₙ. So L is a finite sum of continuous linear maps Λₙ → Λⁿ, i.e. L ∈ (MultiVector P n →L[ℝ] Covector (Euclid P) n). For example, L = Σ_I (ContinuousLinearMap.apply ℝ ℝ (dx^I)).smulRight (dx^I). L does not depend on ξ.
7. (Coefficients of L(ζ).) For J ∈ 𝓘, step 2 gives L(ζ)(e_J) = Σ_I ζ(dx^I)·dx^I(e_J) = ζ(dx^J). Hence |L(ζ)|² = Σ_{J ∈ 𝓘} ζ(dx^J)².
8. (Proof of (b) and (c).) For ξ as in step 5, ξ(dx^J) = s·dx^J(τ) = s·det(τ^J).
 - By step 7 and step 4, |L(ξ)|² = Σ_J s²·det(τ^J)² = 1, so |L(ξ)| = 1 ≤ 1.
 - By linearity of ξ, ξ(L(ξ)) = Σ_I ξ(dx^I)·ξ(dx^I) = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1.
9. (Degenerate cases need no separate treatment.)
 - For n = 0, 𝓘 consists of the empty map, e_∅ is the empty tuple, dx^∅ = 1 and |α| = |α(e_∅)|. Steps 1–8 hold verbatim.
 - If n > P, then 𝓘 = ∅ and step 4 would give 0 = 1. So ℝ^P has no orthonormal family of n vectors, the hypothesis IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q never holds, and the statement is vacuous (L = 0).
proof_key_steps: Define dx^I(v) = det(v_j(I(k)))_{k,j} (SimonGMT wedgeCovectors of coordinate projections); dx^I(e_J) = δ_IJ for strictly increasing I, J.
Expansion α(v) = Σ_I α(e_I)·dx^I(v): both sides are alternating multilinear and agree on all basis tuples.
Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1 for orthonormal τ (Cauchy–Binet), by expanding δ_τ(v) = det(⟨τ_i, v_j⟩) at v = τ.
Cauchy–Schwarz gives |ξ(α)| = |α(τ)| ≤ |α|.
L(ζ) = Σ_I ζ(dx^I)·dx^I is continuous linear, with |L(ξ)|² = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1 and ξ(L(ξ)) = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1.

subproblems.title: Smooth unit-norm approximation of a continuous covector field on a compact set
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (K V : Set (Euclid P)) (β : Euclid P → Covector (Euclid P) n) (δ : ℝ), IsCompact K → IsOpen V → K ⊆ V → ContinuousOn β K → (∀ x ∈ K, covectorEuclideanNorm (β x) ≤ 1) → 0 < δ → ∃ ω : DifferentialForm (Euclid P) n, IsTestForm ω ∧ tsupport ω ⊆ V ∧ (∀ x, covectorEuclideanNorm (ω x) ≤ 1) ∧ ∀ x ∈ K, covectorEuclideanNorm (ω x - β x) ≤ δ

Use in this decomposition: step 6(b) of the sibling mass_identity (Tietze extension, radial retraction, cut-off and mollification of the dual field on a compact K ⊆ W), i.e. the smoothing step of step 3 of the supplied parent proof. The numbered proof below is that node's accepted parent-supplied natural-language proof, copied verbatim.

Source: steps 4(c)–(d) of the parent proof (Tietze extension, radial retraction onto the unit ball of |·|, cut-off, mollification). They are packaged so that only the estimate on K is recorded.
Notation: Λ := Covector (Euclid P) n with operator norm ‖·‖; |·| := covectorEuclideanNorm; 𝓘 is the set of strictly increasing I : Fin n → Fin P, and e_I := (e_{I(0)}, …, e_{I(n−1)}).
0. If K = ∅, then ω := 0 works: it is smooth with compact support, tsupport 0 = ∅ ⊆ V, and |0| = 0. Assume K ≠ ∅ from now on.
1. (The norm |·|.) Let 𝒜 : Λ → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n → Fin P) be the linear map with 𝒜(α)_I := α(e_I) if I is strictly increasing and 0 otherwise. It is continuous (finite dimension), and by the definition of covectorEuclideanNorm, |α| = ‖𝒜(α)‖. Consequently:
 (N1) |·| is continuous;
 (N2) |cα| = |c|·|α|;
 (N3) |α + α'| ≤ |α| + |α'|;
 (N4) |∫ g dm| ≤ ∫ |g| dm for every finite measure m and m-integrable g : ℝ^P → Λ, since 𝒜 commutes with the Bochner integral and the norm of an integral is at most the integral of the norm;
 (N5) |α| ≤ C₀‖α‖ with C₀ := (#𝓘)^{1/2}, because |α(e_I)| ≤ ‖α‖·∏_k ‖e_{I(k)}‖ = ‖α‖.
2. (Tietze.) K is closed and β|_K is continuous. Λ is a finite-dimensional real vector space, so the Tietze extension theorem gives a continuous β̃ : ℝ^P → Λ with β̃ = β on K (Mathlib ContinuousMap.exists_restrict_eq with the TietzeExtension instance RCLike.instTietzeExtensionTVS for finite-dimensional real spaces, or coordinatewise in a basis).
3. (Retraction.) Put ρ(α) := max(1, |α|)^{−1}·α. ρ is continuous by (N1). By (N2), |ρ(α)| = |α|/max(1, |α|) ≤ 1, and ρ(α) = α when |α| ≤ 1.
4. (Cut-off.) K is compact and V open, so there is r > 0 with cthickening(2r, K) := {x : dist(x, K) ≤ 2r} ⊆ V (IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open). Put χ(x) := max(0, 1 − dist(x, K)/r). χ is continuous, 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1 and χ = 1 on K. Since χ(x) = 0 when dist(x, K) ≥ r, support χ ⊆ thickening(r, K) := {x : dist(x, K) < r}.
5. (Continuous unit field.) g := χ·(ρ ∘ β̃) is continuous, with support g ⊆ thickening(r, K) and tsupport g ⊆ cthickening(r, K), which is compact (K compact, ℝ^P proper). Moreover |g(x)| = χ(x)·|ρ(β̃(x))| ≤ 1 for all x. For x ∈ K, g(x) = ρ(β(x)) = β(x), because χ = 1 and |β| ≤ 1 there.
6. (Mollification.) g is continuous with compact support, hence uniformly continuous. Choose s with 0 < s ≤ r such that ‖g(y) − g(x)‖ ≤ δ/(C₀ + 1) whenever dist(y, x) < s. Let φ ≥ 0 be a smooth bump function with ∫ φ dx = 1 and support φ = B_s(0) (Mathlib ContDiffBump (0 : ℝ^P) with rOut = s, normed for Lebesgue measure). Define ω := φ ⋆ g, ω(x) = ∫ φ(t)·g(x − t) dt (Bochner integral in Λ).
 (i) ω is C^∞: it is the convolution of a C^∞ compactly supported kernel with a continuous, hence locally integrable, function (HasCompactSupport.contDiff_convolution_left).
 (ii) support ω ⊆ support φ + support g ⊆ B_s(0) + thickening(r, K) ⊆ thickening(2r, K), using s ≤ r (support_convolution_subset). Hence tsupport ω ⊆ cthickening(2r, K) ⊆ V, a compact set. So ω is C^∞ with compact support (IsTestForm ω) and tsupport ω ⊆ V.
 (iii) For every x, by (N4), φ ≥ 0, |g| ≤ 1 and ∫ φ = 1: |ω(x)| ≤ ∫ φ(t)·|g(x − t)| dt ≤ ∫ φ(t) dt = 1.
 (iv) For every x, φ(t) = 0 unless |t| < s, and ∫ φ = 1. So ‖ω(x) − g(x)‖ = ‖∫ φ(t)·(g(x − t) − g(x)) dt‖ ≤ δ/(C₀ + 1) (ContDiffBump.dist_normed_convolution_le). By (N5), |ω(x) − g(x)| ≤ C₀·δ/(C₀ + 1) ≤ δ.
7. For x ∈ K, g(x) = β(x) by step 5, so |ω(x) − β(x)| ≤ δ by 6(iv). Together with 6(i)–(iii), ω has all the required properties.
proof_key_steps: |·| = ‖𝒜(·)‖ for the coefficient map 𝒜, so |·| is a continuous norm with |∫ g| ≤ ∫ |g| and |α| ≤ C₀‖α‖.
Extend β|_K continuously (Tietze), retract radially onto {|·| ≤ 1}, and multiply by the cut-off χ = max(0, 1 − dist(·, K)/r): g is continuous, |g| ≤ 1, g = β on K, tsupport g ⊆ cthickening(r, K).
Mollify with a normalized smooth bump of radius s ≤ r: the result is C^∞ with tsupport ⊆ cthickening(2r, K) ⊆ V and |ω| ≤ 1 by convexity.
Uniform continuity gives |ω − g| ≤ δ everywhere, and g = β on K.

subproblems.title: Local mass of a current that equals m₀[[M]] on an open set W is |m₀|·Hⁿ(M ∩ W)
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝ^P, T ∈ 𝒟_n(U) (GeometricCurrentOn U n), M, W ⊆ ℝ^P, m₀ ∈ ℤ and ξ : ℝ^P → Λ_n(ℝ^P) (MultiVector P n). Assume: W is open and W ⊆ U; M is measurable; ξ is continuous on M; for every x ∈ M there is a linear subspace Q with IsUnitOrientationOf (ξ x) Q (ξ(x) = ±τ₁∧⋯∧τₙ for an orthonormal basis τ of Q); Hⁿ(M ∩ W) < ∞, where Hⁿ = μHE[n]; and T(ω) = m₀ ∫_M ξ(x)(ω(x)) dHⁿ(x) for every ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(U) (TestFormOn U n) with tsupport ω ⊆ W. Then the local mass satisfies M_W(T) = T.massOn W = |m₀|·Hⁿ(M ∩ W) in [0, ∞] (with |m₀| = m₀.natAbs).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (U : Set (Euclid P)) (T : GeometricCurrentOn U n) (M W : Set (Euclid P)) (m₀ : ℤ) (ξ : Euclid P → MultiVector P n), IsOpen W → W ⊆ U → MeasurableSet M → ContinuousOn ξ M → (∀ x ∈ M, ∃ Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P), IsUnitOrientationOf (ξ x) Q) → μHE[n] (M ∩ W) ≠ ∞ → (∀ ω : TestFormOn U n, tsupport (ω : DifferentialForm (Euclid P) n) ⊆ W → T ω = m₀ * ∫ x in M, ξ x ((ω : DifferentialForm (Euclid P) n) x) ∂μHE[n]) → T.massOn W = (m₀.natAbs : ℝ≥0∞) * μHE[n] (M ∩ W)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 3 of the supplied parent proof ("M_{B_s(z)}(T) = m·H^n(M ∩ B_s(z))"), stated for a general open W and specialized by the parent to W = B_s(z). As in the parent, the upper bound uses the pointwise duality |ξ(x)(α)| ≤ |α|, and the lower bound tests T against smooth admissible forms that approximate the dual field β = sign(m₀)·L(ξ) on a compact set. The only change is in the lower bound. The smoothing lemma is applied directly on a compact K ⊆ M ∩ W chosen by inner regularity, with the open set W itself as the support region. So the auxiliary open set V' and the dominated-convergence step of the parent wording are not needed.
Notation. μ := μHE[n]. For α ∈ Λⁿ := Covector (Euclid P) n, |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α. m := |m₀| = m₀.natAbs. a := μ(M ∩ W), a finite number by hypothesis. For a test form ω put f_ω(x) := ξ(x)(ω(x)). By definition, T.massOn W is the supremum of ofReal(T(ω)) over the admissible forms massAdmissibleOn U n W. These are the ω ∈ TestFormOn U n with tsupport ω ⊆ W and |ω(x)| ≤ 1 for all x.
1. (Duality; sibling orientation_dual.) By the sibling lemma Submission.dor_ims_unitOrientation_dual, fix a continuous linear map L : Λ_n → Λⁿ such that every ζ ∈ Λ_n and subspace Q with IsUnitOrientationOf ζ Q satisfy:
 - |ζ(α)| ≤ |α| for all α ∈ Λⁿ;
 - |L(ζ)| ≤ 1;
 - ζ(L(ζ)) = 1.
 By the hypothesis on ξ, these three facts hold with ζ = ξ(x) for every x ∈ M.
2. (Pointwise bound and integrability.) Let ω ∈ TestFormOn U n satisfy tsupport ω ⊆ W and |ω(x)| ≤ 1 for all x.
 - For x ∈ M ∩ W, step 1 gives |f_ω(x)| ≤ |ω(x)| ≤ 1.
 - For x ∈ M ∖ W, x ∉ tsupport ω, so ω(x) = 0 and f_ω(x) = ξ(x)(0) = 0.
 Hence |f_ω| ≤ 1_W on M.
 - f_ω is continuous on M: evaluation (ζ, α) ↦ ζ(α) is continuous, ξ is continuous on M, and ω is continuous because it is smooth. Since M is measurable, f_ω is a.e.-strongly measurable for μ⌞M (ContinuousOn.aestronglyMeasurable).
 - 1_W is μ⌞M-integrable, because W is open, hence measurable, and ∫_M 1_W dμ = μ(M ∩ W) = a < ∞.
 Therefore f_ω is μ⌞M-integrable (domination by 1_W), and ∫_M |f_ω| dμ ≤ ∫_M 1_W dμ = a.
3. (Upper bound M_W(T) ≤ m·a.) Let ω be admissible for W. Since tsupport ω ⊆ W, the hypothesis gives T(ω) = m₀ ∫_M f_ω dμ. By step 2,
 T(ω) ≤ |m₀|·|∫_M f_ω dμ| ≤ |m₀| ∫_M |f_ω| dμ ≤ |m₀|·a.
 As a < ∞, ofReal(|m₀|·a) = m·μ(M ∩ W), so ofReal(T(ω)) ≤ m·μ(M ∩ W). Taking the supremum over admissible ω gives T.massOn W ≤ m·μ(M ∩ W).
4. (Lower bound: trivial case and sign.) If m₀ = 0, the right side is 0 ≤ T.massOn W. Assume m₀ ≠ 0. Put s₀ := 1 if m₀ > 0 and s₀ := −1 if m₀ < 0, so that m₀·s₀ = |m₀|.
5. (The dual field.) Put β(x) := s₀·L(ξ(x)) ∈ Λⁿ.
 - β is continuous on M, since L is continuous linear and ξ is continuous on M.
 - For x ∈ M, |β(x)| = |L(ξ(x))| ≤ 1, using |−α| = |α| and step 1.
 - For x ∈ M, m₀·ξ(x)(β(x)) = m₀·s₀·ξ(x)(L(ξ(x))) = |m₀|.
6. (Choice of K and ω for a fixed η > 0.)
 (a) The restricted measure ν := μ⌞(M ∩ W) is a finite Borel measure on ℝ^P, since ν(ℝ^P) = a < ∞. Hence it is inner regular on measurable sets with respect to compact sets: finite measures on ℝ^P are Regular, hence InnerRegularCompactLTTop (MeasurableSet.exists_isCompact_sdiff_lt). Applying this to the measurable set M ∩ W gives a compact K ⊆ M ∩ W with μ((M ∩ W) ∖ K) = ν((M ∩ W) ∖ K) < η.
 (b) Apply the sibling lemma Submission.dor_ims_smooth_unit_approx to:
 - the compact set K and the open set W ⊇ K;
 - the field β, which is continuous on K ⊆ M with |β| ≤ 1 on K by step 5;
 - δ := η.
 It gives a smooth compactly supported form ω₀ with tsupport ω₀ ⊆ W, |ω₀(x)| ≤ 1 for all x, and |ω₀(x) − β(x)| ≤ η for x ∈ K.
 (c) Because W ⊆ U, ω₀ is an element ω of TestFormOn U n, and ω is admissible for W. Hence ofReal(T(ω)) ≤ T.massOn W.
7. (Estimate of T(ω).) Let g := m₀·f_ω. By step 2, g is μ⌞M-integrable and T(ω) = ∫_M g dμ. K ⊆ M is compact, hence measurable, so ∫_M g dμ = ∫_K g dμ + ∫_{M∖K} g dμ.
 (a) On K: for x ∈ K, g(x) = m₀ξ(x)(β(x)) + m₀ξ(x)(ω(x) − β(x)). The first term equals |m₀| by step 5. The second has absolute value at most |m₀|·|ω(x) − β(x)| ≤ |m₀|η by step 1. So g(x) ≥ |m₀|(1 − η). Since μ(K) ≤ a < ∞, ∫_K g dμ ≥ |m₀|(1 − η)·μ(K) (setIntegral_ge_of_const_le_real).
 (b) On M ∖ K: |g| ≤ |m₀|·1_W there by step 2. Hence |∫_{M∖K} g dμ| ≤ |m₀|·μ((M ∖ K) ∩ W) = |m₀|·μ((M ∩ W) ∖ K) ≤ |m₀|η.
 (c) Measures: μ(K) ≤ a because K ⊆ M ∩ W. Also a ≤ μ(K) + μ((M ∩ W) ∖ K) ≤ μ(K) + η, so μ(K) ≥ a − η.
 Combining (a)–(c):
 T(ω) ≥ |m₀|μ(K) − |m₀|η·μ(K) − |m₀|η ≥ |m₀|(a − η) − |m₀|η·a − |m₀|η = |m₀|a − |m₀|η(2 + a).
8. (Conclusion.) By steps 6 and 7, ofReal(|m₀|a − |m₀|η(2 + a)) ≤ T.massOn W for every η > 0. As η ↓ 0 the left side tends to ofReal(|m₀|a) = m·μ(M ∩ W), so m·μ(M ∩ W) ≤ T.massOn W. Together with step 3 this gives T.massOn W = m·μ(M ∩ W).

Fix v ∈ V and ε > 0, and write q := ψ(v).
1. Suppose, for a contradiction, that no δ > 0 has the stated property. Then for every j ∈ ℕ the number δ = 1/(j+1) > 0 fails. So there is v_j ∈ V with |ψ(v_j) − q| < 1/(j+1) and |v_j − v| ≥ ε.
2. We have 0 ≤ |ψ(v_j) − q| < 1/(j+1) and 1/(j+1) → 0. By squeezing, ψ(v_j) → q as j → ∞.
3. Let K := {q} ∪ {ψ(v_j) : j ∈ ℕ}. K is compact because it is the range of a convergent sequence together with its limit. Indeed, given an open cover of K, one member contains q, and by step 2 it contains ψ(v_j) for all j ≥ j₀. Finitely many further members cover ψ(v_0), …, ψ(v_{j₀−1}).
4. K ⊆ W. For each j, v_j ∈ V, so ψ(v_j) ∈ ψ(V) ⊆ W. Also v ∈ V, so q = ψ(v) ∈ ψ(V) ⊆ W.
5. By the properness hypothesis applied to the compact set K ⊆ W, the set C := V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact. Every v_j lies in C, because v_j ∈ V and ψ(v_j) ∈ K. C is a compact subset of the metric space ℝ^d, hence sequentially compact. So there are a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ and a point v* ∈ C with v_{φ(i)} → v* as i → ∞. In particular v* ∈ V.
6. Now v* ∈ V, every v_{φ(i)} lies in V, and v_{φ(i)} → v*. Since ψ is continuous on V, it is continuous at v* relative to V, so ψ(v_{φ(i)}) → ψ(v*). On the other hand, (ψ(v_{φ(i)}))_i is a subsequence of (ψ(v_j))_j, so ψ(v_{φ(i)}) → q by step 2. Limits in ℝ^P are unique, hence ψ(v*) = q = ψ(v).
7. Both v* and v lie in V, and ψ is injective on V, so v* = v. Thus v_{φ(i)} → v. Hence |v_{φ(i)} − v| < ε for some i. This contradicts step 1, which gives |v_j − v| ≥ ε for every j, in particular for j = φ(i).
8. So the assumption in step 1 is false. There is δ > 0 such that every v' ∈ V with |ψ(v') − ψ(v)| < δ satisfies |v' − v| < ε. Since v ∈ V and ε > 0 were arbitrary, the statement is proved.

 - ψ(V) = W ∩ M;
 - V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact for every compact K ⊆ W;

By definition (Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_def), μHE[n] = c·μH[n] on every metric space, with the same constant c := addHaarScalarFactor(volume on EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n), μH[n]) ∈ [0, ∞). By the Lipschitz image inequality for Hausdorff measures (LipschitzOnWith.hausdorffMeasure_image_le with d = n ≥ 0), μH[n](χ(E)) ≤ c₂ⁿ·μH[n](E). Multiplying by c gives μHE[n](χ(E)) ≤ c₂ⁿ·μHE[n](E) = c₂ⁿ·volume(E). Here c₂ⁿ = ofReal(c₂ⁿ) = (toNNReal c₂)^(n : ℝ) in [0, ∞].

4. Steps 1 and 3 together are the claim.

 - χ(B_δ(0)) ⊆ M;
 - M ∩ B_{δ'}(z) ⊆ χ(B_δ(0)).
 Let 0 < s < min(δ', (1 − ε)δ), and put r₁ := s/(1 + ε) and r₂ := s/(1 − ε). Then 0 < r₁ ≤ r₂ < δ.
 (a) χ(B_{r₁}(0)) ⊆ M ∩ B_s(z). For |w| < r₁ we have χ(w) ∈ M and |χ(w) − z| = |χ(w) − χ(0)| ≤ (1 + ε)|w| < (1 + ε)r₁ = s.
 (b) M ∩ B_s(z) ⊆ χ(B_{r₂}(0)). Let x ∈ M ∩ B_s(z). Then x ∈ M ∩ B_{δ'}(z), so x = χ(w) with |w| < δ. Hence (1 − ε)|w| ≤ |χ(w) − χ(0)| = |x − z| < s, that is, |w| < r₂.

 Hⁿ(M ∩ B_s(z)) ≥ Hⁿ(χ(B_{r₁}(0))) ≥ (1 − ε)ⁿ r₁ⁿ ω_n = ((1 − ε)/(1 + ε))ⁿ sⁿ ω_n,
